column1: # Ancient Greek for the "Write in ..." tool (scribe.js); built into scribe-langs.js by scripts/make-scribe.ps1.
# rules=greek: the letters from their usual Latin forms (th ph ch ps for θ φ χ ψ, ē/ee for η, ō/oo for ω); an h before
# the first vowel gives the rough breathing, otherwise the smooth one (on the second vowel of a diphthong), an initial ρ
# takes the rough breathing; accents typed on Latin vowels (ó, ò, ô) are kept, a circumflex on o or e means ω or η;
# final sigma; n before a velar is γ. "As on stone": capitals and no marks, as the inscriptions were cut.
# Linear B: the syllabary of the Mycenaean palaces, in its Unicode values (Bennett's numbers in the names).

column4: Greek has been written in its alphabet since the 8th century BCE; before that, the palaces of Mycenaean Greece kept their records in a syllabic script, Linear B.

column2: The Greek alphabet, adapted from the Phoenician in the 8th century BCE; the breathings and accents were added by scholars of Alexandria around 200 BCE, and the inscriptions were cut in capitals.

Type as in the usual romanisation: th, ph, ch (or kh) and ps for θ φ χ ψ, ē for η and ō for ω (or ee and oo), x for ξ. Start a word with h for the rough breathing (hodos → ὁδος). Accents: type them on the Latin letter (ó, ò, ô) or use the keys after a letter. “As on stone” writes capitals without marks, as the Greeks carved them.

column4: theta · t + h (later th as in thin)
sigma · s (ς at the end of a word)
chi · k + h (later ch as in loch)

column2: The syllabic script of the Mycenaean palaces (about 1450–1200 BCE), deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952; its clay tablets were baked, and kept, by the fires that destroyed the palaces.

Type syllables with hyphens, as scholars write Linear B (ko-no-so for Knossos), or a whole word: it is spelt as the palace scribes did, each consonant with the vowel that follows it, with the last consonant and nasals before a consonant left out. Spaces become the short upright word divider.
